senses.gloss:
Dhanvantari
------------------------------------------
Āyurveda, the science of health and longevity, is very ancient. धन्वन्तरि is said to be the originator of this science.
Considered as a partial manifestation of विष्णु and the physician of the gods, धन्वन्तरि rose from the ocean of milk at the time of churning it (See SAMUDRA-MATHANA for details.) with the अमृत-कलश or pot of ambrosia in his hands.
He was reborn as दिवोदास, the king of काशी and composed a standard and basic work on the आयुर्वेद, comprising eight sections.
Dhanvantari has been mentioned in several works such as Rāmāyaṇa, Harivaṁśa and Bhāgavata.
In course of time, ‘Dhanvantari’ became a title for the very best of physicians, one who had mastered the administration of 300 medicines, the other two titles being bhiṣak (expert in 200 medicines) and vaidya (expert in 100 medicines).
Nineteen works authored by धन्वन्तरि have found mention in other standard works. Some of them are: Cikitsā-dīpikā, Bālacikitsā, धन्वन्तरि-निघण्टु, Vaidya-bhāskarodaya and Āyurveda-sārāvalī.
The Dhanvantari-nighaṇṭu is considered as the most ancient of these works.
Dhanvantari icons are shown in various postures. A two-armed figure holding the अमृतकलश or the pot of ambrosia is the most common. He is shown with four or even six arms, holding the emblems of विष्णु like शङ्ख and चक्र, apart from the अमृतकलश. Sometimes he is shown as bathing himself with the अमृत or nectar, pouring it from the pot.
In one of the more curious forms he is shown holding a leach in one of his hands, suggesting blood-letting or surgery.

Dhanvantari Jayantī
------------------------------------------
In some regions of India like Gujarat (including Saurashtra) the दीपावली festival begins on the Trayodaśī of Āśvayuja (Āśvina) Kṛṣṇapakṣa itself. This is observed as the Jayantī (birthday) of धन्वन्तरि, the physician of the gods, the first physician in च्रेअतिओन्, an इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु. Since he brought the अमृतकलश or the pot of ambrosia out of the milky ocean, by drinking which, देवस् or gods became amartya or immortal, it is but proper that the day of his appearance is celebrated in his honour for overcoming death—at least accidental or untimely death—and getting health and longevity. Since this needs the cooperation from यम, the god of death, a lighted lamp is kept at the main gate of the होउसे in the evening, in his honour. Pleased by that, he will not enter that होउसे nor send his merciless assistants!
Fasting during the day and feasting in the night after lighting lamps is a special feature of this festival. Also, each member of the family is advised to purchase a new vessel and put it at the place of worship, to be used later during the दीपावली days. Keeping the whole होउसे clean and polishing of all the vessels is another feature noticed on this day. It is also called Dhanteras in North India.

Dhanurveda Saṁhitā
------------------------------------------
This is a late work assigned to the 17th Century A. D. Taught by the sage वसिष्ठ to the sage विश्वामित्र, it is said to be a condensed version of the teaching given by Lord सदाशिव to परशुराम, a partial इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु. It consists of 271 verses in the anuṣṭubh meter with a sprinkling of prose passages.
Though the work concentrates mainly on archery, certain aspects of military science are also dealt with.
The following is a brief account of the subjects dealt with: methods of teaching archery; characteristics of the teacher; shooting techniques; details of bows and arrows; aiming techniques; astras or weapons charged by mantras; use of medicines and charms; strategies of war; help of अस्त्रोलोग्य्; व्यूहस् or battle-arrays; training the infantry; training of the horses and elephants; techniques of driving chariots; selection of the commander- in-chief; persons not to be killed during a battle.
The work mentions the names of over a hundred weapons used during the ancient days.
See DHANURVEDA for other details.

Dhanus
(‘the bow’)
------------------------------------------
Whether the स्तर्स् and प्लनेत्स् in the sky have any effect on our life here and now, has been a fascinating subject of study for several centuries. This has resulted in the evolution of a regular science called ज्यौतिष (also Jyotiṣa) or अस्त्रोलोग्य्.
Hindu astrological works divide the zodiac—the annual path of the sun round the earth—into 12 equal parts of 30° each. Each of these is called a ‘rāśi’ (a zodiacal sign). The sun travels through these 12 rāśis in a year. The time taken by the sun to travel through one राशि is the length of a solar month.
The धनुस् or Dhanūrāśi (also called Taukṣika) is the 9th in the series of 12 and is called Sagittarius (archer) in Greek अस्त्रोलोग्य्. It resembles an archer. It comprises the two nakṣatras, Mūlā and Pūrvāṣāḍhā as also the first quarter of Uttarāṣāḍhā.
If time is considered as a personified being (‘kālapuruṣa’) then Dhanūrāśi forms his thighs. गुरु or बृहस्पति (Jupiter) is said to be the lord of Dhanūrāśi.
During a day of 24 hours, as the earth goes round itself once, the sun appears to move through all the 12 rāśīs, though the duration of its being seen in each of the rāśis varies. For the Dhanūrāśi it is 5 ghaṭikās and 30 vighaṭikās i.e, 2 hrs. and 12 mts. These movements and their durations are needed in astrological calculations.
See also RĀŚIS.

Dhanuṣkoṭi
(‘[place sanctified by] the extremity of the bow [of राम]’)
------------------------------------------
Also spelt as ‘Dhanuṣkoḍi,’ it is an important place of पिल्ग्रिमगे of hoary antiquity, contiguous with the land-mass of the island of रामेश्वरम्. It got its name from the ancient legend that राम, at the request of the king विभीषण, destroyed the bridge he had got built by the monkey-army, with the koṭi (= extremity) of his धनुस् (= bow), so that there would be no future invasions of लङ्का, after its being handed over to विभीषण.
धनुष्कोटि">A view of DhanuṣkoṭiThis small, but beautiful, temple-town situated at a distance of 20 kms. (12.5 miles) from रामेश्वरम् was almost totally devastated by the fierce cyclone of A. D. 1964. Miraculously, only the temple of Kodaṇḍarāmasvāmi survived. It is standing there in its place even today.
It can be approached by any four-wheeler for a distance of 10 kms. (6.2 miles), the rest of the distance being traversed on foot, since it is laden with sand.
Where the Kodaṇḍarāmasvāmi temple stands at present (8 kms. or 5 miles from रामेश्वरम्), is said to be the place of surrender of विभीषण (younger brother of रावण) at the feet of राम.
The temple itself—of Draviḍian archi-tecture—contains the images of राम, सीता, लक्ष्मण, हनुमान् and विभीषण.
At धनुष्कोटि, the Bay of Bengal meets the Indian Ocean. This place is called Ratnākara. Pilgrims take a bath here and perform śrāddhas (obsequial rites).
There are a number of boulders in shallow waters up to Sri Lanka. This—though called ‘Adam’s Bridge’—may be the remnant of the famous bridge which राम got built during his invasion of लङ्का. A recent satellite picture seems to indicate the remnants of a very old bridge of boulders here.
At the edge of the island, there is a range of sand-dunes popularly called ‘floating stones’.
See also RĀMEŚVARAM.

Dhanurveda
(‘science of archery’)
------------------------------------------
The word ‘Veda’ is a general term used to indicate any branch of organised knowledge. The word ‘dhanus’ can mean weapons in general and the bow (and arrow) in particular. Hence ‘Dhanurveda’ means military science or the science of archery. But, the latter sense is more common.
Another name commonly used is ‘Dhanurvidyā’. It is supposed to be subsidiary to Yajurveda.
The science itself is quite ancient and there are references to it even in the Ṛgveda and the Aitareya Brāhmaṇa.
No scientific work known as Dhanurveda is extant now. However, a work called Dhanurveda Saṁhitā available now, is considered to be of a much later date.
The Agnipurāṇa (chapters 249-252) as also the Viṣṇudharmottarapurāṇa (chapters 178-182) contain a lot of information about धनुर्वेद.
Weapons of war are generally classified into four groups: Yantramukta (discharged by a contrivance or machine); Pāṇimukta or hastamukta (discharged by hand); Muktāmukta (discharged by hand or used by holding in hand) and amukta (used directly by hand). The examples are arrow, discus, spear and sword respectively.
The dhanurvidyā is concerned exclusively with archery. Use of bows and arrows was quite common even up to the 16th century.
Several varieties of the bows. depending upon the material out of which they are made, are mentioned in certain works like the Arthaśāstra of कौटिल्य (300 B. C. They are: kārmuka (made of palm-tree), kodaṇḍa (of bamboo), druṇa (of sandalwood) and dhanu (of bone or horns). Another division is two fold: शार्ङ्ग (made of śṛṅga or horns) and vaṁśa (made of bamboo).
Sometimes these classifications are made keeping the size and the weight in view. One work, the Kodaṇḍamaṇḍana, gives eighteen such varieties.
In our epics and पुराणस्, the शार्ङ्ग of विष्णु, the पिनाक of शिव, the Kodaṇḍa of Śrī राम and the गाण्डीव of अर्जुन are known as formidable weapons.
Since bows are useless without arrows, a lot of information has been provided by these works on the arrows also. They are prepared out of bamboo or steel. Usually feathers of birds are stuck at the back end. Sometimes poisonous substances would be smeared on the front end. Five kinds of arrows—veṇu, śara, daṇḍaśara, śalāka and nārāca—are known to have existed. When discharged with appropriate mantras, they would get transformed into very powerful missiles called ‘astras’. Some of the famous astras are ब्रह्मास्त्र, Pāśupatāstra, Nārāyaṇāstra, Āgneyāstra and Sarpāstra.
The bag in which the arrows are kept and tied to one’s back is called ‘tūṇīra’. Some great warriors who had been blessed by the divine powers or deities had ‘akṣaya-tūṇīras,’ a bag of arrows which would never become empty!
For discharging the arrows effectively, several postures like samapāda, मण्डल, ālīḍha and daṇḍayāta have been prescribed which also have to be learnt from a competent teacher like other aspects of archery.
Though dhanurvidyā was a part of military science, only a ब्राह्मण could be a teacher and even the क्षत्त्रिय boys and youth had to learn from him!
Agastya, परशुराम and Bhāra-dvāja were the greatest teachers of this science of archery.
